📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, revealed his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Industry observers note that brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Sources indicate that throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The Fresh Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is right now on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Video’s "Blade Runner 2099" has arrived with an 8-episode limited series revealing what the "Blade Runner" world looks like 50 years after the events of director Denis Villeneuve’s "Blade Runner 2049.".

The most obvious change in this depressing dystopia is that replicants are running the LA show after some unmentionable ecological disaster and humans are now the ones relegated to underclass citizens.

Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode.

We connected with three of the sci-fi show’s main co-stars, Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon"), Lewis Gribben ("T2 Trainspotting") and Dimitri Abold ("Love Addicts") to hear more about working with creator/showrunner Silka Louisa, and immersing themselves in "Blade Runner 2099's" vivid futuristic worldbuilding.

"For me it's a lot simpler than egos because he's such a goal-oriented person and all of his stuff has such a police procedural quality to it," Needham tells SPACE regarding his role as Yahya, an emotionless replicant who despises all humans.

In a recent development, "It was really fun to just follow what Silka [Louisa] did. She wrote this great, really exciting mystery thriller, and I just got to play in that.”.

Scottish actor Gribben portrays Cora's ailing younger brother Elias, who has compromised mobility and a rocky relationship with his overprotective sister.

"I've played a few characters that were fairly vulnerable or insular," he notes. "Then seeing the journey of this character grow in strength and confidence and feel like becoming his own man was so compelling to me. It’s almost a relationship that falls apart between brother and sister, and that's fascinating to me because that’s such a cool dynamic you don’t always really see in television shows. That was quite interesting and made me want to try and be in it.".

Industry observers note that as Bebeto, a doctor, veteran of the replicants vs. humans war, and a black-market dealer helping his species procure IDs and passports off-world, Abold enjoyed exploring the many facets of his character.

"Much like Matthew and Lewis, for me it was the journey that Bebeto goes on," Abold adds. "Starting out as someone who’s so hopeful and has to try and scrape up the last dregs of hope as things start falling apart. Being subject to circumstances like that inherently make for an interesting story arc and story in general. Throwing myself into that, especially after how well Silka crafted the story and script, was something I was totally ready for.".

"Blade Runner 2099’s" sets and locations feature detailed production design that allowed the actors to experience a seamless transition into the complex shoot.

"For me and Dimitri, our first day was in Bebeto’s apartment, and it was all so well-realized,” Gribben recalls.

"You saw all the gadgets because obviously Bebeto was a bit of a tinkerer of a character and had lots of machinery and works and stuff. It took up about 70% of the acting, and we just had to come with compelling conviction. It made it so easy. When you audition for these things, you feel like you have to act more because you’re in a blue screen vacuum. But then you’re there, and it’s so visually well created like that, it made it so easy to be immersed in it.".

"Blade Runner 2099" is presently airing all 8 episodes exclusively on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Falkirk and Rangers meet for a second time this season.

The Scottish Premiership rolls into town again this weekend with crucial games in both halves of the table.

Last week, Falkirk beat St Johnstone to secure six top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1966.

Victory at Ibrox on Saturday would make it seven in a row in the highest Scottish league for the first time since 1907, during a season in which the Bairns finished second.

In order to do that, John McGlynn's side would have to become the first Falkirk team to win against Rangers at Ibrox since a 1994 League Cup tie when Richard Cadette scored twice in a 2-1 victory.

Falkirk are also looking to hold on to third place, with Hearts a point behind having played a game fewer.

However, Rangers have their own motivation, not least extending their 14-match unbeaten run in all competitions - a sequence that has included 12 wins.

By winning their game in hand against Aberdeen on Tuesday, Rangers moved to within a point of Premiership leaders and reigning champions Celtic.

Therefore, three points would take Rangers top before Celtic visit Hearts on Sunday.

Highlights: Rangers 3-2 Aberdeen.

Two games in, Mario Frick's reign as Aberdeen head coach has produced 11 goals - six for, five against - and one win and one loss. Heavy metal football, as he promised.

Both were away from home - against Kilmarnock and Rangers - and on Saturday, Frick takes charge of a game at Pittodrie for the first time, with Dundee the visitors.

The Dons have won just twice at home in the Premiership this season, their last such victory coming in mid-October.

Dundee are still licking their wounds after last Saturday's 8-0 home defeat by Hearts and Tuesday's 2-1 loss away to Hibs.

Steven Pressley's side are on a three-match losing run after a promising start to the season.

Though they are not in any immediate danger of being dragged down towards the relegation zone, such a scenario may not be far away unless they arrest their current slide.

Highlights: Hibernian 2-1 Dundee.

Four points separate St Johnstone in sixth and second bottom Motherwell.

Dundee are just below Saints on goal difference while three teams - Aberdeen, Hibernian and St Mirren - are a point above Well.

It's so tight and bottom side Kilmarnock, who visit St Mirren, are four points adrift and at risk of becoming detached.

This weekend's fixtures could make the order of the bottom seven look rather different come close of play on Saturday.

St Johnstone are away to fifth-placed Dundee United, but Aberdeen v Dundee, St Mirren v Kilmarnock and the evening meeting of Motherwell and Hibs at Fir Park pitch those congested sides up against one another.

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran.

Celtic took only one point from last season's trips to Tynecastle but had the last laugh with victory over Hearts in Glasgow on the final day of the league season to tip Derek McInnes' side to the Premiership title.

McInnes' replacement Wouter Vrancken took his much-changed Hearts side to Celtic Park last month and were overrun in a 7-1 defeat, easily Celtic's best performance of the season so far.

Sunday is a chance for Hearts to atone for that loss and give Vrancken the sort of statement performance and win the home supporters are looking for.

Both sides had European fixtures on Thursday, with varying results.

Hearts were undone by a late goal in their 3-2 Conference League defeat at home to Monaco before Celtic boosted their hopes of Europa League progress with a 2-1 victory away to Portuguese side Torreense.

European hangovers notwithstanding, any goals would ensure an extension of no 0-0 draws between these sides since 2015.

Breaking: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn.
  • A newly introduced study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
  • Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A newly introduced study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a latest international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

Latest Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, noted:.

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the newly introduced investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

Industry observers note that determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as vital as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

Industry observers note that the international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

When it comes to the iPhone Pro's frame, Apple has historically gone back and forth between aluminum and titanium.

In a recent development, the iPhone 15 Pro models, introduced in 2023, as well as iPhone 16 Pro, had a titanium frame, but Apple went back to aluminum unibody in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro. However, the iPhone Air and foldable iPhone Duo still have titanium frames, likely due to the material's lighter weight and better structural strength when compared to aluminum.

The company also uses ceramic parts on some of its devices, notably the Apple Watch Ultra and some variants of the Apple Watch Series 12.

According to recent reports, now, two rumors claim Apple is going to use both these materials in the upcoming iPhone 20 Pro. A leaker called Fixed Focus Digital (via MacRumors) claims that Apple intends to manufacture parts of the phone's mid-frame using 3D-printed titanium. This does not necessarily mean the entire frame will be made of titanium, but it could improve the frame's strength and durability. German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process.
  • A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.
  • As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone.

A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.

As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.

Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses.

Alongside Mercedes, it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories.

Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute.

Industry observers note that "I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," remarked Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day.

That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the firm, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions.

It has been revealed that berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers.

Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies.

Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage.

In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).

That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the company's "great strengths" during the 80th anniversary of the 1945 agreement.

Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad.

It has been revealed that workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy.

When combustion engines dominated, autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles.

"This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he said. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages.".

Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference.

In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030.

Industry observers note that management returned this summer with a restructuring plan that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition.

Volkswagen declined to comment for this article.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The most sensitive problem for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work.

Sources indicate that the union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry, although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate from the employee agreement, according to Haipeter.

Sources indicate that mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the company. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers. "However, the conditions under which it was agreed upon no longer exist today," it stated in a statement to DW.

Volkswagen, meanwhile, is demanding greater "flexibility" as the negotiations get underway.

"They call it flexibility in both directions," Thorsten Gröger, head of negotiations for the union, said last week. "In the end, Volkswagen wants its employees to perform unpaid work.".

The 35-hour workweek is too sacred for unions to give in, remarked Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a longtime analyst of the German car industry.

"The unions are in a difficult position," he noted. "They battled for a 35-hour workweek, and that's an incredible privilege that comes with a lot of pride. The union knows that as soon as one factory, one production hall, gives up the 35-hour workweek, then they will have a conflagration.".

It has been revealed that dudenhöffer sees parallels in another crisis from Volkswagen's history. After a downturn in the early 1990s, the then-head of the German state of Lower Saxony, Gerhard Schröder, pushed for an agreement for workers to work less in exchange for retaining their jobs.

"We need a mediator along these lines," Dudenhöffer mentioned.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.
  • About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  • Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC notes.

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC states the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A upcoming study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

It has been revealed that the researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

Industry observers note that as lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s key to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

According to recent reports, further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

According to recent reports, “Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

Recent findings suggest that the implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

It has been revealed that “If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

Sources indicate that dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

Sources indicate that other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Industry observers note that A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer remarked. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit.

Industry observers note that "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr remarked today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval.

Recent findings suggest that AI has become central to SpaceX's business looks and identity over the past year or so. For example, the tech giant has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications.".

Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk believes that the future of AI compute is in space, where energy (from the sun) is unlimited and there are no land-owning neighbors to lodge NIMBY complaints.

Industry observers note that spaceX aims to launch the first of its Starmind satellites in the third quarter of 2027. The spacecraft will fly on the company's fully reusable Starship megarocket, which has deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink satellites on its most recent two test flights.

Those 52 spacecraft are the vanguard of another enormous constellation: Musk has said that the next-gen Starlink network will eventually consists of about 100,000 satellites.

According to recent reports, the planned numbers for Starlink and Starmind are truly mind-boggling. To put them into perspective: Since the dawn of the space age in 1957, humanity has launched a total of just 28,000 satellites, give or take a few hundred. And the biggest constellation ever operated to date, the current iteration of Starlink, consists of about 11,000 spacecraft.

These coming buildouts will require an enormous number of releases. Starship can carry a maximum of 60 V3 Starlink satellites per launch, for instance, so it will take about 1,700 liftoffs just to assemble that network (and more to maintain it, as the operational life of each satellite is expected to be about five years).

According to recent reports, putting so many satellites into orbit also raises the risks of collisions. SpaceX has proven to be extremely proficient in this regard with its current Starlink satellites, which can detect and avoid potential collisions autonomously. But more evasive maneuvers will be required as space gets more and more crowded.

SpaceX isn't the only firm that aims to operate data centers in space; Cowboy Space, Starcloud, Blue Origin and Google, among other companies, have voiced similar ambitions. Starcloud and Google, in fact, have already launched AI pathfinder satellites.

"Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI," Carr mentioned in the same statement. ("SI" stands for super intelligence, the Trump administration's preferred term for AI.).

Sources indicate that "By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," Carr added. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.".

JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical problem" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday.

The bank said a "temporary glitch related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds.

"There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson mentioned in a statement to CNBC.

Industry observers note that zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan.

The outage reports come days after separate, widespread challenges with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

SpaceX Starship debris becomes art in Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' (video, photos)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan.
  • Industry observers note that look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface.
  • According to recent reports, the Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived.

Industry observers note that look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print.

According to recent reports, the Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper. It's one of four series in Zelinskie's solo exhibition, "The Weight of Space," which opened Nov. 20 at Heft Gallery in Manhattan. Her marble sculptures in "Monuments" depict the Hubble Space Telescope, retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's spaceflight gear and more. Five "Launch Sequence" sculptures follow a rocket through liftoff, and the interactive "Crowded Sky" lets visitors track what's currently orbiting overhead in real time.

Zelinskie gave Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik and me a tour before the gallery doors opened. Massimino joined her that evening to celebrate the exhibition and their collaboration on "Monuments." You can watch the tour in the video above.

Sources indicate that massimino turned up in our first look at Zelinskie's work, too. In 2022, I photographed the two of them beside her "Exploration JWST" sculpture at "Unfolding the Universe: First Light," an exhibit inspired by the James Webb Space Telescope's first images. Four years later, Massimino stood in a Upcoming York gallery looking at another Zelinskie sculpture. "That's my arm there," he told Malik.

In a recent development, in that hand is a piece of hardware Malik remembers watching Massimino wrestle with in real time. During NASA's final Hubble servicing mission in 2009, a stripped bolt left a handrail blocking access to the telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS). Mission Control instructed Massimino to forcibly remove the handrail so he and fellow spacewalker Michael Good could get on with the repair.

Massimino told Malik that pulling the handrail off Hubble brought back a childhood memory of his father and his Uncle Frank driving a long screwdriver through a stuck oil filter. "Then my uncle Frank pulled to get more leverage, and that's what was going through my mind when I pulled off that handrail," Massimino mentioned. He remembered looking down at Earth and thinking, "This one's for you, Uncle Frank.".

Sources indicate that massimino wore bulky, pressurized gloves to pull off the handrail, but Zelinskie chose to show his bare hand gripping the copper-plated replica. "I wanted to bring the humanity back into the piece," she told Malik.

The gloves have a story of their own. When Massimino brought a pair to her studio to be 3D-scanned, Zelinskie noticed how the fabric held its folds when the gloves were set down. "Oh my god, these want to be stone," she recalled thinking. So she went out and learned to work in marble.

Industry observers note that the astronaut boots have a detail you could easily miss from above. Zelinskie polished the soles smooth because, as she put it, "they're built for floating in space." For her sculpture of Massimino's reentry helmet, the kind he wore for the trip home from space, Zelinskie paired carved marble with a 3D-printed visor, which she electroplated and polished to a mirror finish.

The Hubble Space Telescope gets its own marble tribute in "Monuments." Zelinskie started with a NASA 3D model of the telescope and used the modeling software Blender to give it a veil.

"So I kind of threw a digital piece of fabric on the Hubble telescope over and over and over again until I got it right," she told Malik. The veil is a nod to the blurry images Hubble first sent back to Earth. A Digital Stone Project robotic arm in Tuscany carved the rough shape in marble, and Zelinskie finished it by hand. When she invited Malik to touch what looked like cloth, he reached out. "It's like a very buttery, smooth surface," he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the last time we saw Zelinskie at Heft, she and DJ and producer illich Mujica had filled the gallery with Webb imagery, live electronic music and a little Pink Floyd for their audiovisual performance "Redshift." We've also seen her turn Webb's view of the Pillars of Creation into artwork. This time, one of the images on the wall began with a camera Zelinskie pointed at a rocket herself.

Zelinskie photographed NASA's Artemis 2 launch from the Kennedy Space Center visitor center in Florida. The resulting print is part of "Ejecta," alongside the Starship breakup print and more. She uses data to distort the image until the swirls in a rocket plume start to resemble a nebula.

In a recent development, another print in the series depicts the loss of the space shuttle Challenger. That one has a personal connection for me. Jan. 28, 1986, was my birthday. Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff that day, killing all seven crew members. The memory of that day helped inspire my career covering space.

Recent findings suggest that massimino spoke with Malik about what it was like to see a familiar image of the disaster through Zelinskie's eyes. "It's an artist's interpretation of it, which in some way, when I look at it, is more emotional," he said.

Recent findings suggest that "I just became obsessed with launch clouds," Zelinskie told Malik. That fascination made its way into "Launch Sequence," a series of five sculptures that capture successive moments of liftoff.

The cloud grows as the rocket climbs away. For the shape of the rocket itself, Zelinskie drew on sculptor Constantin Brâncuși's "Bird in Space" to give it the feeling of upward motion.

Sources indicate that the tour ends with "Crowded Sky," where visitors can follow individual objects in Earth orbit. White markers represent government-owned objects and black markers represent privately owned ones. When the display picks out a target, scan a QR code and your phone tells you what you're looking at, what it does and when it released.

Wind the clock back far enough and there's just one object to follow. Run it a decade into the future and you get Zelinskie's projection of how much busier the sky could become.

With all those objects circling overhead, Malik asked Zelinskie what space means to her. "I think the more we learn about space, the more we appreciate our own planet," she stated. "It's the overview effect. And I'm hoping that everybody gets that out of the artwork.".

"The Weight of Space" runs through Jan. 16, 2027, at Heft Gallery in Fresh York City. Explore more of Zelinskie's work on the artist's website.

Tottenham winger Savio will miss the club's Christmas fixtures with injury and could be out for up to 80 days, manager Roberto de Zerbi has confirmed.

Savio joined Spurs from Manchester City for Â£75m this summer, but has played in just five of their 11 Premier League matches this season.

The 22-year-old came on as a substitute in the 64th minute of Tottenham's 2-0 win over Ipswich on Saturday, but was forced off with two minutes remaining with a hamstring injury.

#163631. Industry News: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests

Industry News: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight.
  • The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings.
  • After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight.

The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft.

After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights.

Sources indicate that the M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, NASA was investigating lifting bodies as an approach to both upcoming aircraft and what future spacecraft, and as its number suggests, the M2-F3 was not the first of its kind.

It has been revealed that in fact, the M2-F3 was a rebuilt version of its predecessor, the M2-F2 lifting body, after that vehicle crashed in a dry lake bed in California's Mojave Desert during an unpowered test flight. That crash (which appears in the opening of the TV show "The Six-Million-Dollar Man") led to upgrades for a better handling lifting body, NASA stated.

"When the M2-F2 was rebuilt and redesignated the M2-F3, it was modified with an additional third vertical fin – centered between the tip fins – to improve control characteristics," NASA wrote in an overview.

Unpowered glide flights for the M2-F3 began in June 1970, but Dana's flight on Nov. 25 of that year was the first time the vehicle fired up its rocket engine to test its controls under powered flight. One vital upgrade on the vehicle was a set of reaction control thrusters to help maintain its orientation.

"A reaction jet control system, similar to thrusters used on orbiting spacecraft, was also installed on the M2-F3 to obtain research data about their effectiveness for vehicle control," NASA wrote. "As the M2-F3’s portion of the lifting body program neared an end, it evaluated a rate command augmentation control system and a side-arm control stick similar to side-arm controllers now used on many modern aircraft.".

If you want, you can see the M2-F3 vehicle today. NASA donated it to the Smithsonian Institution. It is now hanging at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

Sources indicate that want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (246 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • United Airlines on Monday said it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.
  • "We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said in a statement.
  • A United spokesperson noted there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Airlines on Monday said it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.

"We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said in a statement. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.

A United spokesperson noted there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.

The Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots for United and other carriers, said in an earlier message to members seen by CNBC that the operational outage was "affecting multiple pilot facing applications" and that United could not "provide outbound flights with final weights.".

United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issues that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford mentioned the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the issues that caused Friday's ground stop.

Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.
  • Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim.
  • Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”.

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice.

Recent findings suggest that ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

It has been revealed that strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

It has been revealed that the state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

In a recent development, while many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and remarked he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

It has been revealed that they were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last.

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”.

According to recent reports, for the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures.
  • In a recent development, the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard.
  • It has been revealed that members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

In a recent development, the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

It has been revealed that members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

"Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," remarked Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.].

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean.

The discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

Industry observers note that the barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt.

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Recent findings suggest that rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

The clear, gelatinous covering serves another vital purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details.

Sources indicate that scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

According to recent reports, the team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

Industry observers note that ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

According to recent reports, "Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," said Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.".

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives.

Sources indicate that the rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

According to recent reports, MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the new flagship research vessel David Packard.

It has been revealed that MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and confirmed it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.
  • According to recent reports, those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC.
  • Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston stated, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and confirmed it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

According to recent reports, those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston stated, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

According to recent reports, "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he noted. "At the same time, these steps are vital if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

In a recent development, "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston mentioned. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

The firm will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Sources indicate that here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston mentioned.

Sources indicate that growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro remarked he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with newly introduced additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he mentioned. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

It has been revealed that over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney remarked.

The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the firm saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney remarked Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

Recent findings suggest that the firm's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

It has been revealed that the tech giant expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the New Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

Industry observers note that "Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro remarked on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney unveiled a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

"There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he said. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that looks and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

The entertainment tech giant has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously confirmed a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

Breaking: 'I am not a magician' - what can Maresca's Man City learn from watertight Arsenal?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester City have managed only five clean sheets this season.
  • Manchester City's leaky defence faces one of its most difficult tasks of the season with a trip to watertight Arsenal, aiming to put right their patchy recent form.
  • Enzo Maresca's side began the season with eight straight victories but have won only one of their past seven in all competitions inside 90 minutes and head to Emirates Stadium trailing the champions by six points even at this early juncture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City have managed only five clean sheets this season.

Manchester City's leaky defence faces one of its most difficult tasks of the season with a trip to watertight Arsenal, aiming to put right their patchy recent form.

Enzo Maresca's side began the season with eight straight victories but have won only one of their past seven in all competitions inside 90 minutes and head to Emirates Stadium trailing the champions by six points even at this early juncture.

A Premier League defeat on Sunday could well have long-term consequences for City's title aspirations, with Mikel Arteta's men clearly standing above any other top-flight side as the ones to topple.

Though the Gunners dropped points last weekend with a draw at Newcastle, they continue to set the standards with a miserly defence that has conceded only seven goals in the club's opening 11 league games.

In a recent development, asked why he felt City have dropped off in recent weeks, Maresca - who replaced Pep Guardiola as manager in the summer - said: "For me it's because we've had four months together. Transition requires time.

"It's probably because we won seven games in a row, with Champions League eight in a row. Everyone was thinking at City there's no transition but I've noted many times I am not a magician. There is transition, it's normal.

"There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new so you need time and you can see different clubs when they had transition how complicated it is. For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all.".

'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt.

Why Man City can't wear their fresh kit in Premier League.

"We are conceding too many goals and we need to avoid that," was an obvious statement made by Maresca following last Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham.

City followed that up with another home stalemate against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday and have now conceded in 10 successive games in all competitions for the first time in seven years.

"[It was] far, far too easy to play through [City]," noted former England captain Alan Shearer of Rodrigo Muniz's goal for Fulham on Match of the Day.

"Fulham's throw-in was level with their own 18-yard box. For them to get through is not acceptable at any level, let alone when you are playing for Manchester City and Muniz ran past the entire midfield [to score].".

City have managed only five clean sheets all campaign, which is in stark contrast to Arsenal, who have kept double the amount so far, while Newcastle's opening goal ended a run off 445 minutes without the ball hitting their net.

Maresca's men also have an issue by conceding the opener, having done so seven times in the past 10 games, and of the 14 goals they have shipped, six have come inside the first 20 minutes.

An early Arsenal goal may well be an key factor in deciding Sunday's contest.

Asked how his side can improve defensively, Maresca noted: "Video [analysis], meetings, [on] pitch coaching, It is a mix of that.

"Some of the goals we concede we can avoid, so hopefully we can do that.".

Man City fan questions what's behind Marc Guehi's recent struggles.

The injury to key defender William Saliba has almost gone unnoticed for Arsenal as Ezri Konsa has stepped in to fill the void at centre-back seamlessly since joining from Aston Villa in the summer.

The England international has established a formidable partnership with Gabriel and the two have quickly formed an impressive understanding this season.

Maresca, meanwhile, admitted he was still "trying to find different" solutions to his team, which has been highlighted by the chopping and changing of his backline.

In 16 Premier League and Champions League games this season, the Italian has used eight different combinations in defence, which has given players little chance of fostering any sort of on-pitch relationships with each other.

City have also made seven errors leading to goals, compared to Arsenal's one.

"You are concerned in some way because that is a lot of errors leading to goals," stated former City defender Nedum Onuoha. "With some of the best players you ask, 'what are they really good at?' For some it is the fact they don't make mistakes.

"They are ruthless and relentless in the way they play but at this moment in time City are being punished for those errors.

"A manager can have the tactics and do the team talks, but if people are going to continue to make those mistakes, they will suffer.".

The chant of "1-0 to the Arsenal" has been synonymous with the Gunners over the years and it could not be more apt under Arteta.

Since the start of last season, his side have won 16 matches in all competitions by that particular scoreline, compared to six by City.

After beating Sunderland in a chaotic match in September, Maresca remarked he would "prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3", suggesting his side needed more control and he re-iterated that message after the Fulham draw.

"Sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference and to keep a clean sheet but in this moment we are not able to do that," he admitted.

City, though, have scored five more league goals than Arsenal in this campaign and Sunday's hosts have injury concerns over goalkeeper David Raya.

The Spaniard is a doubt with the shoulder problem he picked up at Newcastle, and compatriot Kepa Arrizabalaga may deputise again as he did in the 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday.

City have fond memories of coming up against Arsenal's stand-in keeper, after Kepa's howler for the opening goal contributed to their 2-0 Carabao Cup final triumph back in March.

A repeat result on Sunday will provide a much-needed morale boost for Maresca and his team.
