Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance.
  • In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.
  • The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. Fresh research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.

The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an key role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," mentioned Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Industry observers note that rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

How Scientists Simulated Overtraining.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

According to recent reports, one group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

In a recent development, overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

According to recent reports, for the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

Industry observers note that after the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours.

Recent findings suggest that in mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This indicated that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

The more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

Sources indicate that this prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than promptly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

However, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

It has been revealed that dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

According to recent reports, another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

This result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body.

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

Sources indicate that excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The new results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another crucial part of this process.

Sources indicate that for recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

Rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he right now works as a researcher.

Industry observers note that additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

According to recent reports, the team is now participating in a newly introduced international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac.

Industry observers note that december's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

According to the late, great astronomer Fred Espenak, the Cold Moon will be just 221,667 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth when it turns full, making it the closest supermoon of 2026!

Recent findings suggest that the full Cold Supermoon will make for a spectacular sight when it rises over the eastern horizon at sunset on Dec. 23, mere hours before reaching maximum illumination. Remember to use Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location.

Earth's satellite may appear larger than normal while close to the horizon. This is partly because it is near perigee, when it appears subtly larger in the night sky, but also because of a phenomenon called the moon illusion, which tricks us into perceiving the moon to be bigger than it actually is while in the presence of foreground objects.

The moon may also adopt a striking golden or orange hue around moonrise and moonset. When the moon is low on the horizon, its light travels through more of Earth's atmopshere, scattering shorter, bluer wavelengths of light and allowing longer, redder wavelengths to reach our eyes.

The December full moon is often called the Cold Moon in reference to the often freezing temperatures that can descend this time of the year. It's also known as the "Long Night Moon" by the Mohican tribe of North America, because of its proximity to the winter solstice, which marks the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

Old English peoples knew it as the "Moon Before Yule", according to Time and Date, while the Celts of Europe referred to it as the Oak Moon after traditions that centered around the hardy trees.

The December full moon also coincides with the Hindu festival of Datta Jayanti, when followers gather to celebrate the birth of Lord Dattatreya, who embodies the Hindu holy trinity of Lord Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, according to the Government of Maharashtra. The December full moon also rises close to the Christian celebration of Christmas on Dec. 25, when followers celebrate the birth of Jesus Christ.

Sources indicate that the Cold Moon will shine in the center of a majestic "Winter Hexagon" of stars bright enough to easily cut through the glare cast by the lunar disk after it rises on Nov. 24.

Begin by locating Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky, which rises into the southeastern sky shortly after 8 p.m. local time for viewers in Upcoming York. Next, trace an imaginary line to the blue supergiant star Rigel in the nearby constellation Orion, before hopping to the orange glow of Aldebaran, which represents an eye of the great bull depicted in the constellation Taurus.

Next we move to Capella, the jewel of the constellation Auriga, before jumping down to Pollux in the constellation Gemini and nearby Procyon, before closing the loop with Sirius once more.

Industry observers note that jupiter and the red light of Mars will shine low in the eastern sky in the hour before midnight, while Saturn will lurk close to the western horizon. Look to the southeast just before dawn to spot Venus appearing as a brilliant "Morning Star", with the red giant Arcturus shining higher in the predawn sky close to the constellation Bootes.

The December full moon presents a stunning opportunity to photograph the lunar disk as it shines in Earth's sky entirely free from shadow. Want your research cited in patents? Publishing open access increases your chances

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paywalled papers are cited less frequently in patents than are open-access studies.Credit: Eoneren/iStock via Getty.
  • It has been revealed that open-access science publishing is having an impact far beyond the academic sphere.
  • An analysis of almost 500,000 patents, and the research papers they cite, has shown that open-access papers were cited 1.38 times more often than would be expected on the basis of their prevalence in scientific papers1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paywalled papers are cited less frequently in patents than are open-access studies.Credit: Eoneren/iStock via Getty.

It has been revealed that open-access science publishing is having an impact far beyond the academic sphere. Industries that rely heavily on scientific discoveries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, disproportionately cite open-access work in their patents over paywalled research, a study has found.

An analysis of almost 500,000 patents, and the research papers they cite, has shown that open-access papers were cited 1.38 times more often than would be expected on the basis of their prevalence in scientific papers1.

In a recent development, when the study authors expanded the definition of open access to include papers available on Sci-Hub, a website that hosts pirated copies of scientific articles, this over-representation was even stronger. Papers that were freely available (either through the journal publishers or Sci-Hub) were 3.41 times more prevalent in patent citations than they were in the wider scientific literature.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in Scientometrics, show how heavily inventors lean on open-access research, says study co-author Abdelghani Maddi, a scientometrics researcher at Sorbonne University in Paris. When you include platforms such as Sci-Hub, “the numbers are striking”, he says. “Open science is not only about who can read science, it’s about who can build on it.”.

For their analysis, Maddi and his colleagues leveraged the ‘Reliance on Science’ data set, a publicly available tool that identifies citation links between patents and journal publications2. They found that research-intensive industries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, cite the scientific literature (both open and pay-walled) in their patents much more heavily than do more engineering-based industries, such as vehicle- and construction-equipment manufacturing.

The researchers also showed that patents from countries with a high proportion of high-tech industries, including South Korea, Singapore and Denmark, cite more scientific publications than do those from countries with more heavy manufacturing industries, such as South Africa, Brazil and Italy.

To track patent citations of open-access papers specifically, the team cross-referenced research publications in the Reliance on Science patent database against those in OpenAlex, an index that catalogues hundreds of millions of scientific documents. They then used a normalization metric to account for differences in open-access publishing practices across research disciplines. Open-access publishing is much more prevalent in the health sciences than it is in computer science, for example, states Maddi.

According to recent reports, seeing how open-access papers were over-represented in patent citations suggests that making research freely accessible does more than just help people to read and share scientific findings, states study co-author Francesco De Pretis, an applied mathematician at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia in Italy. It also makes that knowledge more likely to be used in developing new technologies and inventions, he adds. “Our findings show that open science is not just a matter for academia, it’s also the business of industry and of national economies.”.

According to recent reports, matt Marx, an innovation and entrepreneurship researcher at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, whose team developed the Reliance on Science database, states the finding that patents tend to cite open-access papers “is especially intriguing”. But he cautions against assuming that ease of access is the only factor at play. “Perhaps inventors are more likely to cite papers they can read because those are open access, or it could be that prominent or crucial papers are more likely to be open-source,” he says.

According to recent reports, regardless of the exact causes, the access barrier is real, says Marin Dacos, who heads the open-science taskforce in France’s Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Space. Negotiating contracts with thousands of journal publishers worldwide requires specialist library staff — a resource that is generally only available to large companies and universities, he says.

#163618. A Fresh Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1331 w)

A Fresh Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.
  • Sources indicate that to rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build fresh data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia.
  • An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German organization Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a upcoming breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.

Sources indicate that to rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build fresh data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia. But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components, and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.

An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German organization Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a upcoming breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.

Whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.

According to recent reports, the aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.

Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud company IONOS as part of a pilot program. It says that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a latest class of hardware.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Sources indicate that WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?

Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.

If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a latest processor that takes care of the heavy math.

The cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.

Sources indicate that how would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?

It has been revealed that light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function. [The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.

Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.

What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?

The Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.

According to recent reports, linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.

We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.

What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?

I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.

According to recent reports, under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.

Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?

There’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.

In a recent development, but if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.

According to recent reports, it’s a chicken and egg problem, right? Until developers are building models to run on this type of processor, it’s going to be difficult to sell them to cloud providers. Equally, until photonic processors are available for people to use, it’s going to be tough to convince developers to design for them.

Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology, it will need time to get the credibility and trust that’s needed for a firm like Google to build data center infrastructure around it.

That’s the reason we chose to go into data centers with proof of concept systems, to validate that photonic computing is robust enough to withstand that environment.

We want to invite the world to compute on our systems. We are building a upcoming chicken, so you can start producing eggs. Let’s find out together whether they’re tasty or not.

What else should I understand about why photonic processors are not already widely in use?

If hypothetically we received an order of 100,000 [photonic processors], we at Q.ANT are ready, but I’m not sure about the suppliers.

Recent findings suggest that hardware is not software. On the assembly side, it will need [time] before we have the same robust supply chain as the semiconductor world.

Do you expect to suffer from the same problem as other hardware challengers in securing capacity with the big chip manufacturers?

Sources indicate that [To produce Q.ANT chips] you only need 90 nanometer node technology, from the 2000s. A lot of foundries already use this capability to produce chips that are super cheap. With this technology, you can use the same line to produce high-performance chips with a much higher street price, without massive upfront investment in your assets.

That resonates well with the industry.

Are Q.ANT processors built to function alongside a particular brand of GPUs—say, Nvidia or AMD—or are they totally agnostic?

Industry observers note that there’s no need to go single-sided with a particular GPU. We want to have the freedom to cooperate with any of them.

Either way, we are not competitive to GPUs, we complete their function set.

Can you imagine a future in which AI models run entirely on photonic processors, or will they always be a sidekick?

Recent findings suggest that if we see an opportunity in five years to attack the GPU as well, we would not be shy about taking it. But at the same time, I do not know what workloads in five years are going to be like.

It depends on the architecture of future AI models, you mean?

Could the chance to perform certain calculations more cheaply with photonic processors change the way that AI engineers design future models?

The core message is that we need to do something to fight the energy cost in the AI stack.

That’s where we see the future of AI: very data-optimized models that allow for tasks of the same quality, but at a fraction of the energy—and therefore a fraction of the operating cost.

  • UN Women Germany is one of 13 UN Women national committees worldwide, each an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization committed to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.
  • Their current campaign "Orange The World" runs from the start of International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25 to December 10, International Human Rights Day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Domestic violence has reached a record high in Germany, with 16 women subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors each hour.

UN Women Germany is one of 13 UN Women national committees worldwide, each an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization committed to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.

Their current campaign "Orange The World" runs from the start of International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25 to December 10, International Human Rights Day. It is designed to raise awareness around violence against women in the country and worldwide. The 2026 campaign's focus is particularly on men's responsibility in ending gender-based violence.

"In these 16 days of activism, we can deliver a lot of information. Survivors of gender-based violence can find out where to get support and be reminded that they are not at fault," UN Women Germany chair, politician and long-standing campaigner for women's rights Elke Ferner told DW. "The debate helps and it's a chance to change consciousness about the topic.".

According to recent reports, germany captain Giulia Gwinn remarked in a statement via the German Football Association (DFB): "Violence against women and girls affects us all and must have no place in our society. As the women's national team, we therefore want to once again use our reach to create awareness for this vital issue and jointly set a visible sign against violence.".

The campaign with the women's team is not new. Two years ago, the team joined the campaign, delivering a moving video that saw players reveal the truth of statements by crossing out words.

During Germany's upcoming South America tour — part of their preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil — they are to wear special UN Women Germany badges on their sleeves in their games against Argentina and Peru.

It has been revealed that ferner believes the work with role models is pivotal and that the campaign is powerful, especially in a football context. A 2022 study from Warwick Business School in the UK revealed alcohol-related domestic abuse rises by nearly 50% after England's men's football team win a World Cup game, never mind lose.

Currently, there is no data on domestic abuse during Germany games, however during the 2026 World Cup last summer, Berlin police recorded a 31% increase in domestic violence compared to the week before.

Ferner is encouraged that sport has understood the importance of the matter, and that the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) and other sports clubs and organizations are helping move the conversation forward.

According to recent reports, in sport, this is particularly important given the problematic nature of dependency relationships that so often exist in high-performance environments. But violence against women is really a societal concern that is not specific to class, origin, religion or societal space, such as sport.

It has been revealed that "Violence against women has structural origins and to change that you need to change the structures," Ferner said. "You just need to do it. I always say, this isn't about a lack of knowledge but rather a lack of action.".

Performance is an integral part of sport, but a multi-dimensional understanding of it might help shift perspective in a country that remains driven by a performance culture.

"What is performance? Higher, faster, further? Or is it managing to look after a family of three?" Ferner asked. "Why do people who repair washing machines earn more than those looking after your kids in nursery? This is about changing business culture, but also awareness around the role men play at home and in the family.

It has been revealed that "The picture boys and young men get of girls and women in school is a problem that needs addressing. We can't wait for generational change. This is about saving lives. We need to change societal structures.".

Industry observers note that sports structures are also in need of reform. Non-profit organization Safe Sport provides independent support for people affected by sexual, physical and psychological violence in both amateur and professional sport in Germany.

They are the only organization with a specific focus on violence in grassroots sports in Germany, and one of only two in professional sport in the country. They also have to contend with structures, in a sporting context, that make spaces less safe for women.

"Gender roles have become more fluid in the last few years, but in associations and clubs management positions are still occupied by men, regardless of the sport," Safe Sport manager Ina Lambert told DW.

"In professional sport, there are a lot fewer women involved in training and so the space remains male dominated, and, as a result, so do the power structures.

"We have people in search of advice, men included, who see the problems and want to enforce change, and we offer them support so they are not alone," Lambert remarked. "But whether in a big association or a small club, perpetrators are frequently protected, incidents are ignored and so the people who want to enforce change are often prevented from doing so.".

Safe Sport, which provides free psychological and legal support, has only been in action since July 2023, but in that time the number of support requests they have received continues to grow. Psychological violence in sport in Germany is the most common case they are faced with, but sexual violence is also a major problem.

"There is finally recognition of the problem and there is a seriousness about tackling it," Lambert said.

"There is a lot of good work being done in the right direction, with many good concepts for prevention, intervention and processing violence, as well as more education, holistic training and focus on women's menstrual cycles.".

Sources indicate that germany's Interior Ministry is leading the process with participants from the country's states, organized sport, affected parties and academia to create a central hub. The center for safe sport was founded in July 2026, but investigative and sanctioning work is expected to begin in the spring of 2027.

It has been revealed that support from leading figures clearly makes a huge difference, but it's also clear that more data is needed. Addressing the underlying issues, such as social norms and gender stereotyping, is a must.

Sources indicate that after all, as UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous said: "No country has yet eliminated violence against women. Ending it requires transformative action — greater investment, innovation, and unwavering political will.".

What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jamal Musiala came off the bench with 14 minutes remaining in Bayern's defeat by Lille on Wednesday.
  • Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.
  • During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jamal Musiala came off the bench with 14 minutes remaining in Bayern's defeat by Lille on Wednesday.

Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.

During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.

This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.

At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical matter had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.

In a recent development, but it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".

In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.

Sources indicate that soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an matter. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.

According to recent reports, after the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.

However, his comeback lasted just two games - he came off the bench in Bayern's 1-1 Bundesliga draw against Cologne, and in the Champions League defeat by Lille, but the club confirmed on Friday that he has torn his right hamstring and will be out until further notice.

On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training, Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.

All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.

It has been revealed that absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.

Sources indicate that A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.

The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.

"He has a health concern, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer.".

A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.

Hoffmann, a neurologist, stated it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.

One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.

Industry observers note that he might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.

But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.

Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.

Recent findings suggest that musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.

Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.

In a recent development, under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, Â£21m a year, with Â£15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to Â£25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.

Some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract only offers sick pay for six weeks before insurance would shoulder the payments.

But even six months is a short period in comparison. Premier League players receive their full basic wage for the first 18 months. And, when Bayern negotiate with top players, they ultimately compete against Europe's elite.

Rummenigge, and to a lesser extent his long-time boardroom compatriot Uli Hoeness, made Eberl responsible for the unfavourable terms - arguing that Schmid essentially played Eberl.

Eberl has been the target of criticism from the two former powerbrokers for quite some time. At a recent supervisory board meeting, Hoeness is mentioned to have attacked Eberl for his inactivity over the Musiala issue in the past six months.

That being said, Bayern bought into the Musiala hype for a couple of years, hoping that they would have a superstar of their own who could be marketed across the globe.

The relationship between the club and agent Schmid has been strained to say the least, with Rummenigge particularly disliking him. Some sources believe this was one of the root causes for Rummenigge's recent attack on live TV.

Industry observers note that when a 16-year-old Kennet Eichhorn came on the market during the summer, as he wanted to leave second-division side Hertha Berlin, Bayern were interested but ultimately dropped out of the race for the highly touted midfielder. Eichhorn is represented by Schmid and ended up joining Bayer Leverkusen.

Bayern boss Vincent Kompany (left) has himself recently been diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Hoeness met with Schmid during the summer to discuss how to proceed with Musiala, but the player's agent did not indicate that they would agree to a wage reduction. Hoeness called the matter a "dilemma" for Bayern during a TV show earlier this month, but did not go as far as Rummenigge.

Industry observers note that as long as Musiala is not medically forced to retire, he will receive the wage that was agreed upon in February 2025. Even if Bayern would intend to part ways with the player, they would need to do everything in their power to get the player as close to his previous form as possible.

Industry observers note that the release clause of Â£125m, which could be triggered next year, seems unrealistic. Any comments by Bayern bosses against Musiala, or further leaks to the media, may indeed lower his market value down to zero - unless the player can simply shake things off and perform again.

Eberl and head coach Vincent Kompany have come out to back Musiala. Joshua Kimmich, one of Bayern's veteran players, also criticised the treatment of Musiala after a 2-1 loss to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday. "Of course, the club is above all and bigger than the player, but not bigger than the human. This is an absolute no-go and also not Bayern-like," Kimmich said.

Even football players' union Fifpro condemned Rummenigge's comments. On Wednesday, Bayern put out a statement saying that a meeting between the club and Musiala's representatives took place on Tuesday, in which it was agreed that the player's health should be paramount.

It has been revealed that whether the damage can be repaired is up in the air. As Bayern have a number of attacking players sidelined, they need a healthy and mentally prepared Musiala in the coming weeks and months.

#163614. Breaking: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (917 w)

Breaking: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared.
  • During the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different.
  • The newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. The strange animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has also received a name with a personal connection to the two student scientists who helped identify it.

During the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different. Instead of a modern city, the landscape was a warm, swampy river delta populated by giant insects, early animals adapted to life on land, and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways. This environment supported an extraordinary variety of life, leaving behind fossils that now provide a remarkable glimpse into Earth's prehistoric past.

The newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. Its name means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek," honoring the mothers of the two student researchers, both of whom are named Jean. The discovery is described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

A 309-Million-Year-Old Fossil With Extraordinary Detail.

The Mazon Creek fossil deposits are among the world's most crucial sources of Carboniferous fossils, in large part because of the conditions that existed when the animals were alive.

Sources indicate that as plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment quickly covered their remains. This rapid burial created ideal conditions for fossilization, sometimes preserving delicate structures that would ordinarily disappear long before they could become fossils.

"What's really cool about Mazon Creek is that it preserves all of these unusual details -- things like toe pads and body outlines," claims Allison Sefcovic, co-lead author of the paper and 2025 Women in Science intern at the Field.

Recent findings suggest that "In the fossil of Jeanerpeton, we can see some of the scales on its back and tiny 'belly ribs' called gastralia. You can even see the eye impressions! It's so cool to see.".

According to recent reports, these exceptionally preserved features offer valuable evidence of what early amphibian relatives looked like. They also indicate that several anatomical characteristics associated with modern frogs and salamanders were already present approximately 309 million years ago.

A Prehistoric Species Hidden in Plain Sight.

Sources indicate that although Jeanerpeton mazonensis has only recently been formally described, its fossil was discovered many years earlier. An amateur fossil collector originally found the specimen and later donated it to the Field Museum.

When researchers first examined it, they classified the animal as Amphibamus grandiceps, a previously established species known from the Mazon Creek area. However, closer examination eventually revealed that the fossil represented a distinct animal.

According to recent reports, misidentifications like this can occur when scientists have limited information about ancient species. Fossils that appear similar are sometimes assigned to an existing species even when notable differences have not yet been recognized.

Paleontologists refer to such broad classifications as a "waste bin taxon." The term describes a category in which multiple fossils are grouped together because they seem related, even though their true identities and evolutionary relationships remain poorly understood.

"What we're finding from the Field Museum's collection are a bunch of things that historically were grouped together into this waste bin taxon known as Amphibamus grandiceps," indicates Cam So, co-author on the study and postdoctoral researcher at the Field Museum.

"Jeanerpeton is one of those species. And now, we've found enough evidence to support it being an anatomically distinct animal. With this publication, we officially pull Jeanerpeton out of this waste bin taxon.".

According to recent reports, the finding highlights how museum collections can continue to produce discoveries long after fossils are first collected. In this case, a specimen already held by the Field Museum provided enough anatomical evidence to establish a separate species.

Two Student Scientists Make a Remarkable Discovery.

The research was co-led by Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who participated in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. The initiative encourages young women to explore careers in scientific research and museums.

Both students worked alongside So as members of the research group led by Arjan Mann, the museum's assistant curator of fossil fishes and early tetrapods in the Negaunee Integrative Research Center.

For Kohlberg, the project offered an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar scientific field and gain confidence through hands-on research.

In a recent development, "Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," says Kohlberg. "My experience at the Field and in the Women in Science program has made me more confident in my abilities to try something newly introduced. It is scary to take on a project when you feel like you don't know as much as you should, but I learned with my practical experience that it is possible to overcome that fear with hard work.".

It has been revealed that the identification of Jeanerpeton mazonensis adds another species to the growing record of ancient life preserved at Mazon Creek. As researchers continue examining fossils from the region, each discovery helps reveal more about the extraordinary diversity of animals and plants that inhabited Illinois more than 300 million years ago.

These are the animals people most want to see photographed

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions.
  • Sources indicate that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo.
  • However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Massive Five” for wildlife photography.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability complications and to inspire positive action.

Sources indicate that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Massive Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Massive 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green states that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on problems impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he notes.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”.

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change.

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, notes Green.

It has been revealed that “I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”.

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, notes Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “Newly introduced Significant 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds.

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, mentioned in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she remarked.

“The Latest Massive 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of concerns covered by the book.

#163610. Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (916 w)

Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same.
  • The study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles.
  • Recent findings suggest that when sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same. Researchers at Adelaide University have now identified a surprising reason for this dramatic change, offering insights that could help make hydrogen-powered stoves, ovens, and other household appliances safer and more dependable.

The study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles. Sea salt transported inland by the wind is one important source.

Recent findings suggest that when sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow. But when sodium concentrations fall, the flames become much harder to see, even though the burner continues operating under the same conditions.

This discovery has notable implications for the development of hydrogen appliances. Instead of depending on flame color to show whether a burner is running, engineers may need to incorporate other detection technologies. Improving these systems could help support the adoption of hydrogen as a lower-emissions alternative to natural gas.

Why Hydrogen Flames Change Color With the Weather.

Lead researcher Professor Paul Medwell, from the School of Electrical and Mechanical Engineering at Adelaide University, explained that studying hydrogen flames under ordinary environmental conditions is essential for developing appliances that people can safely and confidently use at home.*.

"Hydrogen has significant potential as part of a lower-emissions energy future, and we need to understand how it behaves in the real world if we want people to be confident using it.

"Our research helps explain why hydrogen flames can look different from one day to the next. That knowledge gives engineers valuable information to develop appliances and flame-detection systems that work reliably, regardless of changing environmental conditions.".

Industry observers note that to investigate these changes, the researchers combined controlled laboratory experiments with outdoor testing around Adelaide. They examined how hydrogen flames responded to variations in atmospheric conditions, including shifting weather patterns and changes in the air reaching the burner.

In a recent development, over two weeks, the team monitored light emissions from hydrogen flames while keeping the burner settings unchanged. Despite the consistent operating conditions, the sodium-related light signal varied by more than 28 times between its lowest and highest recorded values.

Weather played a major role in those differences. Air that had passed over the ocean generally contained more sodium, producing flames with a stronger orange glow. When the air carried less sodium, the flames appeared considerably fainter.

Hydrogen Flames Are Harder to See Than Natural Gas Flames.

The researchers also examined how hydrogen flames compared with those produced by a conventional natural gas cooktop.

They found that hydrogen flames emitted less visible light on average, even when atmospheric conditions favored a brighter flame. This difference presents an additional challenge for appliances that use visible flames to indicate whether a burner is operating.

Industry observers note that hydrogen combustion can also produce faint blue and red light. However, the researchers found that these colors were easiest to detect in darkened surroundings, making them less useful as reliable visual indicators under everyday lighting conditions.

According to recent reports, together, the findings show why judging whether a hydrogen burner is operating based on appearance alone may be unreliable. A flame that is clearly visible under one set of conditions could become extremely difficult to detect when the surrounding air changes.

Making Hydrogen-Powered Homes Safer.

Medwell emphasized that the results do not undermine hydrogen's potential as an energy source. Instead, they demonstrate why appliances must be engineered to accommodate the fuel's particular properties.

"Different energy sources have different properties, and good engineering is about understanding those differences and designing for them.

"Rather than relying on a flame looking a particular color, we can investigate other ways of confirming that a burner is operating. Options include specialized ultraviolet or infrared flame detectors and temperature sensors.

"By identifying the factors that influence flame visibility, we can help inform the development of hydrogen appliances that are fit for purpose in real homes and other everyday settings.".

Such detection systems could provide a more dependable way to confirm that hydrogen is burning, regardless of whether its flame appears orange, faint blue, or is barely visible.

By identifying how environmental sodium affects flame visibility, the research provides information that engineers can use when designing hydrogen appliances for kitchens and other everyday environments. That knowledge could help make the technology safer and more practical as interest in lower-emissions energy alternatives grows.

Recent findings suggest that the project brought together researchers from Adelaide University, the University of Latest South Wales, and Gas Infrastructure Research Australia. Support came through the Future Fuels Cooperative Research Centre, with funding provided under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program.

The study, 'The role of sodium on hydrogen flame visibility in domestic settings,' was published in Next Energy.

*In 2023, the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) introduced Australia's first 100% hydrogen-powered home in Victoria. The demonstration showed that household gas appliances could operate entirely on hydrogen, a development described as a 'game changer'.

According to recent reports, materials provided by Adelaide University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The independent commission is yet to decide on a sanction for Manchester City.
  • Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for it breaking financial rules, senior figures at some Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.
  • This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The independent commission is yet to decide on a sanction for Manchester City.

Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for it breaking financial rules, senior figures at some Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.

This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.

The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.

Now, officials at three top-flight clubs have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.

Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue.

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City.

The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.

But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.

Industry observers note that in comments that reveal the level of anger felt by other clubs, another source claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by Â£900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.

Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.

According to recent reports, the official - who also spoke anonymously - remarked that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.

Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or stated they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.

But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.

In a recent development, it also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".

When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently remarked that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.

Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.

According to recent reports, "Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan noted.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

Recent findings suggest that "But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?".

Sheikh Mansour's control of Manchester City has come into question.

When asked how any potential legal battles with Manchester City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs that a litigation reserve of Â£2m was to be built up over the next two years via the levy charged to clubs, which would be paid back if litigation was successful.

According to recent reports, "Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than Â£2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular", Monks added. "So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.

"We'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way.".

Last month it was revealed that the IFR would cost clubs in the top five divisions of English men's football Â£20.3m annually.

According to recent reports, last week, Premier League clubs voted to cover legal expenses for its five board directors if any of City's sponsors sued them. Two UAE-based commercial partners - Etihad and Etisalat - have both mentioned they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

Recent findings suggest that the IFR has the authority to force a sale within section 34 of the Football Governance Act which allows it to investigate whether an owner meets the required suitability standards around honest, integrity and financial soundness. If an owner fails this assessment, the regulator can direct them to take reasonable steps to relinquish ownership within a specified period before issuing an ownership removal order.

It has been revealed that city have been approached for comment. The club previously said that the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe", adding that they filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home Depot on Tuesday announced its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.

Industry observers note that alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot remarked Ann-Marie Campbell, right now senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.

Industry observers note that decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The tech giant remarked on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.

Recent findings suggest that "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession blueprint.".

McPhail has been with the manufacturer since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.

"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.

Industry observers note that he said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.

It has been revealed that home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the firm has previously noted it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.

Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.

Sources indicate that the CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The organization mentioned comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.

Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.

Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period.

"We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail noted on the call with analysts.

In the third quarter, the organization noted online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.

The tech giant mentioned it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.

Sources indicate that for the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase.

Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

#163603. Industry News: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1425 w)
